about: The words of the chain pilots_secret (Data/encounters/chain_pilots_secret_793.json; Design/content/chains/pilots_secret.md): every title, intention, line and label the fourteen cards use, an outcome text for every option (out_<option>, with _success and _failure for a chance; named in each option's note), five news items, and a picture line for every card (art.<card id>). Gerlef, Wilsuit and Gerbrand are the people of the Witla places file; Thiadbod and Count Folcbert are the spine's. The verse of the marks is invented in the period's manner (a list said as verse; 'the work of giants' is what the English called Roman stone). Nothing is quoted from a book: Bede on the tide and the Acts on sounding are given in our own words. A draft for the user to overwrite. Written 6 Oct 2026.

entries.text: The man who watches the bar
The pilot of the Maas mouth sits in the door of his net shed and watches the bar. Skippers offer him silver to take them over it. Nobody asks him how he knows.
She runs north of the bank since the floods. You came in on last year's marks with a hand's breadth under you. I watched. I do not often get to watch that twice.
Do not ask me to take you out. Thiadbod's ship is looked for, and he pays me by the year to be free for her. I never said I liked it.
Four ships wait on this ebb and each master has a purse out. They all want to be taken over. Not one of them wants to know where she went.
The post stands well clear of the ridge end this morning, father. Anybody can see that.
Grandfather, why do the gulls stand in a row out there, when there is all that water to sit on?
Because they have something to stand on. That is the first question anybody has asked me this year that was about the water.
Sit down and ask where the channel went this winter
Offer him forty pennies to show you the marks
Carry his pole and line down to the boat, row for him, and say nothing

He talks until the flood is half made: where the old channel filled, where the river cut a new one, which bank is walking south. He does not look at you once. When you get up he says: come again when you have sold your cloth. I have more water than this.

He looks at the forty pennies as a man looks at a fish he did not order. Thiadbod offered a pound, he says, and I told him what I tell you: it is not for silver. Sit down or go away. You keep your pennies.

You row him out and back through one tide while he sounds for a wine ship. He says nothing to you that he does not say to the water. On the strand he counts six pennies of the fee into your hand and says: you pull evenly. Come again.
The far mark
A wine ship stands in for the bar. The pilot asks you, as if it did not matter, whether the post on the dune is open of the ridge yet. It has been open for some time.
The far mark is soft this year. It is the haze. It was the haze last year too.
That will be the red sail from Colonia. No? Striped. Then it is the light. A striped sail looks red in this light.
What a lot of room there is between the post and the ridge today. And a striped sail coming in, a hand north of where she should be.
I talk too much. Everybody says so. It is a great help to him.
You asked me about the water. So I ask you about the mark. That is all it is.
Say what you see, the way his daughter does: as if by chance
Tell him plainly that you saw him miss it
Say nothing here, and sell the word in the ale-houses up river: the pilot of the Maas is going blind

You remark on the post, the ridge and the striped sail, to nobody. He brings the ship in by what you say and what the pole tells him, and she never touches. Afterwards he says a Dane once paid his fee with a riddle about fog, and gives it to you. It is as near as he comes to thanks.

He says nothing for the length of a tide. Then: so you know what I am selling, and why I am in a hurry. He is short with you until dark. In the morning he is plainer with you than he is with his own daughter.

Three skippers at Dorestat pay ten pennies each to know it before the others do. One of them is Thiadbod's man. At Witla the pilot's daughter hears who brought the word up the river before your boat is back in the creek.
Not silver
After Michaelmas the wine ships stop coming and the pilot has time. He has you sit on the net pile and says what he wants for the marks. It is not silver.
My father had the Maas from his father. I had the Vlie from my wife's father, with her. Each of them told one man. A thing two men know is a thing for sale.
My price is three things. A spring, a summer and an autumn of your boat, when I say and not when the market says. Your mouth shut about my eyes. And the boy.
He is too young to carry it and I am too old to wait. So you carry it. When he can hold the pole you put it in him, all of it, and you ask him nothing for it.
You said it to my face, about the mark. So I need not pretend with you. That saves a tide.
Somebody sold my eyes in the ale-houses up river. I do not ask who. I ask you to swear, and I will listen to how it sounds.
I am forty. I have been forty for some time. There is no hurry, except that there is.
The pole, yes. Not the sea. Teach him the bar and leave him the shore to sleep on. That is my part of the price, and nobody asked me for it.
Swear it at the cross on the ridge, with your hand on his pole
Give him the three seasons, and swear nothing about a boy you hardly know
Swear it, and pay Thiadbod back his year so the old man is nobody's but the water's

You swear at the cross with the wind taking the words, your hand on the notched pole and his hand over yours. He gives you a riddle to hold until spring: the answer, he says, is the only friend a ship has on this coast. Then he says: after Easter, on the first quiet ebb. Bring oars.

He thinks about it for as long as it takes to mend a mesh. A man who will not swear will at least not lie to me, he says. You will have the water. The boy we will see about. After Easter, on the first quiet ebb.

You swear at the cross, and you count sixty pennies into his hand to send up the river: what Thiadbod pays for a year of him. He holds them a long time. Twenty years I have been rented, he says. I had forgotten I was for sale back. He gives you a riddle to hold until spring, and his daughter sends ale after you to the boat.
After the floods
The winter floods have moved the bar again. On the first quiet ebb after Easter the pilot goes out to find where the channel went, and this year he takes you to be his eyes.

Forget marks. Marks are what is left over afterwards. First the pole. Then the lead, and look what the tallow brings up: grey sand is the bank, shell is its edge, black mud is the old channel and she has left it.
Where gulls stand at half ebb there is a hand of water. Where she is brown and smooth she runs deep. Where she wrinkles with no wind on her, keep off.
And she is deepest here when a full moon stands in the south-east. That is the one thing my father told me that is still true.
Seven hands. Seven. Six and a thumb. Grandfather, it goes shallow the wrong way round.
Pilot! I have forty casks of the bishop's wine and I have been looking at your beach for two days. A full fee to whoever brings me in before I drink the cargo.
You may take him in if you think you have her. But if you put him on the bank it is my name that lies on the strand, not yours. Say now if you are not ready.
Take the pole yourself, and let him say what the tallow means
Row for him three ebbs and learn by watching
Bring the wine ship in yourself, under his ear, for the fee

You sound and call; he names what you bring up before you have finished saying it. By the turn of the tide you have her: a crooked road of brown water north of the bank, eight hands deep. He takes two ships over it that evening and gives you twenty pennies of the fees. You found her, he says. I only recognised her.

You read shell where there was sand, and your own boat sits down on the bank and starts a plank. Fifteen pennies to the wright, and the crew look at the sky. The old man is not angry. Now you know what sand feels like through a pole, he says. Again tomorrow. You find her on the second ebb.

For three ebbs you row and he sounds and the boy calls the notches. You say nothing and miss little. It takes longer this way, and nobody goes on the bank. On the third evening he has you point to where she runs, and you point, and he says: north of that. But not much.

You stand in the wine ship's bow with the pole and the old man stands behind you with his head on one side, listening to the water along her planks. She comes over the bar on the last of the flood and never touches. Her master pays ninety pennies and rolls a cask down the plank after them. The old man says: do not tell me you were not afraid. I could hear it. Good.

She takes the bank a ship's length short of the deep and sits there a whole tide with forty casks in her. Nothing is broken but the day. You pay her master thirty pennies for it, and on the strand they say the old pilot put a wine ship ashore. He lets them say it. You sound the bar again, and this time you have her.
Rented by the year
On the dam at Dorestat Thiadbod is friendly, which is how you know he wants something. He has heard that his pilot has taken a pupil.
I pay Gerlef by the year. A man I pay by the year does not give away in spring what I paid for in winter. You see how it looks, neighbour. I only say how it looks.
You sent me back his year. Sixty pennies, in a cloth. It was neatly done. I counted it twice, to be sure I was not being thanked.
So let us be plain. What he puts in your head, you put in my steersman's. A hundred and fifty pennies today. And when you have the Vlie as well, something better than pennies.
They say in the ale-houses his eyes are going. Then he is selling a cask with a hole in it, and you and I should agree a price before the news is any older.
I can learn a bar in a tide. It is only water.
Tell him the marks were never his to buy and are not yours to sell
Take the hundred and fifty pennies, and promise him the marks when you have them all
Say the old man teaches nothing: he only talks to the water

Thiadbod goes on smiling, which costs him something. As you like, he says. I rented a pilot for twenty years and never once thought to ask him anything. It seems that was the cheaper way to get it. He does not offer you ale.

A hundred and fifty pennies, counted on a cask head, in good new coin. Thiadbod's steersman watches them go into your purse as a man watches his own dinner carried past. When you have the Vlie, says Thiadbod. I am patient. Ask anyone I have lent to.
Thiadbod laughs. Then he talks to it for a long time, he says, with you sitting in the boat. He lets it lie. He is not deceived, only put off, and he has time.
North along the dunes

Between Whitsun and Lammas the weather is as steady as it gets. The pilot stands on the strand with his pole and a bag of bread. The Vlie, he says, is three days north with the dunes on your right hand, and he has not seen it in twelve years.
I had the Vlie from my wife's father, on the Westflinge side. She is dead and so is he. If the water there has moved since, nobody thought to send me word.
He does not go out alone at dusk any more, and now he is going to the Vlie. Bring him back before Lammas, and bring him back dry.
I can call the lead. I call it better than he hears it. Ask him.
There is the inside way: up the river, down the Vecht, over the Almere. Sweet water and no bar. Saint Boniface went that way to be killed. You learn nothing on it.
Take the old man and the boy, outside along the dunes
Take the old man outside along the dunes, and give his daughter your word on Lammas
Take him by the inside way: up the river, down the Vecht and over the Almere

The boy is in the bow before anybody has said yes. His mother stands on the strand with her arms folded and does not wave. The old man sits in the stern with his face to the wind and says: north. Keep the dunes where you can count them.

You give your word on Lammas and she takes it as she takes a penny, looking at both sides. The boy is left on the strand with the old pole. The old man sits in the stern with his face to the wind and says: north. Keep the dunes where you can count them.

His daughter kisses your sleeve. The old man gets into the boat as a man gets into a cart. Up the river, then, he says, with the cows. You will see the Vlie from behind, like a thief. He does not say the verse of the dune marks on a river, and you do not hear it.
The verse of the marks
The dunes go by on the right hand, one pale hill like the next. The old man cannot see them. He says them in order, in a verse, and after each line he asks you whether it is there.

The post on the ridge, and the Maas behind you. A day of white dunes with never a tree. A stone in the surf that the giants squared, where the Rhine goes out tired. Kinnem's sand, and the saint's roof behind it. Then the dunes lie down and the land goes low: that is the door of the Vlie.
A verse, because a verse can be said in the dark and in a gale. And because when a line is lost you can hear the hole. Nobody can tell when a list is short.
The stone. Is it there? Say what you see, not what I said.
It is there, grandfather. But there is white water a long way south of it. More than is in the verse.
If there is white water south of the stone, the Rhine is shutting her door. My father took ships in there. That is why the line says 'tired'. One day it will have to say 'dead'.
Say the verse back to him, line by line, until it holds
Cut the marks on a yew stick at night, where he cannot see you do it
Hold your tongue, steer, and learn the shore with your eyes

You have it by the time the saint's roof is abeam: five lines, each with a thing in it you have now seen. He has you say it once more with your eyes shut. That is how I say it now, he says. It is no worse.

You lose the third line, then the fourth, then the third again. He has you say it nine times. By the ninth the whole crew has it and the man at the bailer is saying it under his breath. Good, says the old man. Now it is in five heads and I must drown four of you.

At night under the tilt you cut it small along a yew stick: post, dune, stone, roof, door. The knife is quiet. In the morning he says: you were cutting something. A tally, you say. He turns his face to you. I am going blind, he says, not deaf. A tally does not take that long. He says no more about it.

You let the verse go by like the dunes and learn the shore itself: the stone in the surf, the white water south of it, a small grey roof behind Kinnem's sand, the place where the land lies down. He knows you are not saying it. Eyes are good, he says, while they last.
Her door has moved

The Vlie is a narrow water between the Frisian shore and Wiron, with the lake behind it. The old man says the channel lies under the eastern bank. A fisherman mending an eel trap says it has lain under the western one since before his son was born.
Under the west bank, and narrower every year. The king's man takes his tenth from every keel that finds it. The keels that do not find it pay the mud.
Twelve years. I gave you a verse and the last line of it is a lie. Do not be kind about it. I do not know this water.

The king's tenth, and of that a tenth to Saint Martin at Traiectum. His boat comes for it after harvest and goes aground every second year. Find her a road and the saint will not be the only one grateful.
Good. Now you can learn the only part worth having. Not where she is. How to ask her.
A verse goes bad like fish. I should have told you that when I gave it to you. I did not know it myself until this morning.
Try my old marks if you like. You will find out the hard way how many of them still stand. I would not. But I am not the one who is learning.
Lie here three tides and find the channel yourself, with pole, lead and tallow
Pay the fisherman twenty pennies to take you through and name his marks
Try the old man's marks, to learn how much of the verse still stands

Three tides. Grey sand, grey sand, shell, then black mud, and the water going brown and smooth along the western bank. You find her without one mark that anybody gave you. The old man sits in the stern and says nothing at all, which is new. Saint Martin's boat comes down on the fourth tide and you take her through. The toll-gatherer pays forty pennies, halves your toll until autumn, and asks for four casks of wine by a keel that will not sit on his doorstep.

The fisherman takes you through in the time it takes to say it: the dead alder, the trap stakes, the hut with one wall. You have this year's road for twenty pennies. The old man says: now you know where she is. Ask him where she will be after the next ice. He will not know either, but he will not be surprised.

The eastern marks are gone or lying, and you know it within a ship's length. So you stop trusting them and feel for her with the pole, across the stream and back, as he taught you on the Maas. She is under the west bank. The old man says: one line of mine was still true. Which? None, you say. He laughs for the first time since Witla. The toll-gatherer pays forty pennies for the saint's boat brought through, and orders wine.

The old marks put you on the mud at the top of the tide, which is the worst time for it. You sit there until the next one, through a cold night, with a cask stove and thirty pennies of goods spoiled. The old man does not speak. At first light the fisherman hauls you off and names his marks for nothing: he says he has not had so good a night's watching in years.
The tide in a book

At Saint Martin's the schoolmaster has heard that a shipman knows why the saint's boat goes aground at Medemelacha. He has a book open at a page about the moon and the sea, and a boy beside him with a pen.

Bede the priest wrote it at Jarrow in my grandfather's day. The sea follows the moon, and each day the flood comes later by four parts in five of an hour, as she does. He says every shore has its own hour and the men who live on it know it. He did not write the hours down. Nobody has.
You carry in your head what he left out. Say it, and the boy will write it on the last leaf, after the tides. Saint Martin's boats would stop feeding the mud.

It is no heathen craft. Saint Paul's shipmen let down the lead and found twenty fathoms, and a little further on fifteen. It is in the Acts. They also wished for the day, which I take to be the oldest prayer at sea.
This parchment is hairy and the ink is thin. But I can write 'sand'. I can write 'mud'.
You swore to tell one boy. I ask you to tell one book. A book does not gossip. It is, I grant you, easier to carry off.
Say the marks, bar by bar, and let the boy write them
Give them only the hours: where the moon stands at high water on each bar, and no marks
Say it is in your head on loan, and not yours to put on a leaf

You say it and the boy writes it: a rough leaf for now, in a hand like a row of fence posts, to be made fair later. The schoolmaster reads it back to you in Latin and you know your own bar by the sound of it. The cellarer sends sixty pennies. Walking down to the boat you find you have learned what 'arena' is, and 'lutum'.

The moon in the south-east for the Maas; a little later for the Vlie. The hours belong to no man: any fisherman has them. The boy writes two lines under Bede's page and the schoolmaster is as pleased as if you had given him a relic. He reads you the whole chapter in return, slowly, and the cellarer sends thirty pennies.

The schoolmaster shuts his mouth on what he was going to say, and then nods. A thing held in trust, he says. We have a word for that too. He reads you Bede's page on the sea and the moon all the same, slowly, putting each sentence into Frisian, and asks nothing for it.
A space beside the Maas

The count has a list of the river mouths between the Sincfal and the Vlie, and beside each a space for the name of a man who can take the king's boats in. Beside the Maas the space is empty, and somebody has told him about you.
Shipman. The Maas mouth. I am told one old man knows it, that Thiadbod rents him, and that you are learning it for nothing. That is three things I dislike, in one breath.
In the Lent before he went to Rome, the lord king rode the shore himself and ordered ships and a watch against the pirates. A watch that cannot cross its own bar is a row of men looking at the sea.
The king's toll boat at Witla went on the bank twice last year. The second time the toll was in her.
Put your name in the space. Teach two of my men the bar. A hundred pennies now. Later, when I am asked who keeps the king's river mouths, I say your name and not Thiadbod's.
You Frisians say you need follow the king no further than the Weser and the Vlie, out with the ebb and home with the flood. I am asking you to go as far as your own doorstep.
Put your name beside the Maas, and take the hundred pennies
Say the marks are the old man's to give, and the old man is not giving
Say the bar moves every winter: let the king's men come at Easter and sound it with the rest of us

The clerk writes your name beside the Maas, and after it a word you cannot read. A hundred pennies are counted out from the toll chest. The count says: when you have it all, shipman. I can wait a year. The king is said to be less patient than I am.

The count looks at you as at a horse that has stopped. An old man on a beach, he says, and the king's ships wait on his pleasure. He does not threaten. He has the clerk leave the space empty, which is worse.

The count breathes out through his nose. The clerk, who has been at Witla, writes one word in the space. What have you written, says the count. 'Moves', lord, says the clerk. It is the truest thing on the list.
The first winter he has not sounded
The pilot does not get up when you come to the shed. He turns his face to the sound of your feet in the shells and says your name. The pole stands against the wall with this year's notches uncut.
It went at Michaelmas, between one tide and the next. I can still tell flood from ebb by the sound. That is not enough to take a ship in on.
You have all I had, and the one thing I did not have until the Vlie showed it to me: that the verse goes bad. Now. Three men have asked me whose the marks are. I told each of them: ask him.

You stayed away, and I could not wait for you. Sit. What I cannot show you I will tell you from here, and you will have to go and see how much of it is still true. It is not the way I meant. Then: whose are they to be?
You swore to me with your hand on the pole. I am not reminding you. I am only saying where the pole is.
And you have a stick. I heard the knife, the second night. I have been waiting ever since to hear what you would do with it.
Wilsuit says the priests at Traiectum have me on a leaf. An old man, pressed flat. Well. It is done. What is left is whether it is done properly.
The boy asks after you every time a sail shows. He has outgrown two poles since you first came.
I sounded the bar myself after the last gale. I found two channels. I think one of them is wrong, and I do not know how to ask him which.
Keep faith: come back for the spring sounding and put all of it into the boy
Have it written, the bars and how to find them, so that it cannot die in one head
Tell him the marks will have a master up the river: the count, or Thiadbod

He nods once, towards the bar. After Easter, then, he says. The first quiet ebb. The boy will hold the pole and you will row, and I will sit in the stern and be in the way. His daughter puts a bowl in your hands before you have asked for one.

He is quiet a long time. A leaf does not move, he says, and she does. But a leaf does not go blind either. Do it, then. Only have them write at the top, before anything else: she moves. If they will write that, I do not mind the rest.

He does not turn his face away, since it makes no difference to him where it points. So it was for sale after all, he says. I held it forty years and never found that out. His daughter takes the bowl she had brought you back into the house. The boy is sent to look at the nets.
The pole changes hands

On the first quiet ebb after the floods a boat goes out to the bar at Witla: the grandson in the bow with the pole, you at the oars, and in the stern a place for the old man, if he is still above ground to sit in it.
Do not tell me what you see. Tell him what to ask. I am only here for the air.
Grey sand. Shell. Shell. Black mud: she lay here last year and she has gone. She is north of us. Is she north of us?
Sound it twice, boy. The first time is for the river. The second time is for you.

He died in the hard frost after Martinmas, sitting with his face to the bar. He said your house asked about the water first. It was the best he said of anybody. Then he said: if that one comes, he knows where the pole is.
What he did not get to put in you, I can. And what you saw that he could not, you can put in me. It is the same water.
He has the pole and he sleeps at home. That is the bargain I wanted, and I did not think a merchant would be the one to keep it.
I know who carried the word about his eyes up the river. I have not told the boy. See that I never have a reason to.
Give the boy everything you have, and take your half of the season's fees
Give him everything, and stand at the cross as his foster-father in the craft: your house and the pilot's, one kin
Take the marks as your wage, pilot for yourself this summer, and leave the boy to what the old man told him

From Easter to Lammas you and the boy take every keel that asks, he with the pole and you behind him saying less each week. By Lammas you are saying nothing. Your half of the fees is three hundred pennies; the skippers' thanks are four casks of wine and six bolts of cloth. The Maas mouth and the Vlie are yours to cross without asking anyone. On the strand they have stopped calling him the old pilot's boy.

At the cross on the ridge, before the priest and the strand, you take the boy by the hand and say that his house and yours are one kin in the craft: what one knows the other is owed, to the last heir. All summer you and he take every keel that asks. Five hundred pennies, six casks and eight bolts are your part. The old man's lead is put into your hand, the tallow still in its foot. Keep it, the boy says. I have the pole. It ought to be in two houses.

You take the ships in yourself that summer, for the whole fee: six hundred and fifty pennies by Lammas, and a lead and line of your own. Nobody on the strand has stopped you and nobody on the strand speaks to you. The boy sounds the bar with what a blind man could tell him and goes on the bank twice before he has it. He will be a good pilot. He will not be your friend, and neither will his mother.
The leaf after the tides
In the writing room of Saint Martin's a leaf lies ruled and empty at the back of the book of times, after the chapter on the sea and the moon. The schoolmaster asks what, exactly, is to go on it.

Nobody in the North has written a shore down. The Greeks did it for their own sea, I am told: we have the word for such a book and not one of the books. This will be a single leaf. I should like it to be a true one.
Your stick is very well for a man who reads sticks. I can make out 'dune'. Read it to the boy, and slowly.
Thank God it is one leaf. My hand is tired of the moon.
One thing troubles me. You say the bar moves each winter. Then what I write at Martinmas is false by Easter, and a false leaf in a true book is worse than an empty one.
Unless we write what you say you learned at the Vlie. Not where the channel is. How a man asks the water where it is.
Write whatever keeps my boat off the mud. I will pay for the calf.
Dictate the verse and this year's marks, bar by bar
Dictate the way of asking the water, and a rule: a brother sounds each bar at Easter and amends the leaf
Dictate it, and have a second leaf made for the boy at Witla, so the pilot's house has what the saint has

The verse, the post, the stone, the roof, the western bank of the Vlie: one leaf, in a fair hand, with 'she moves' at the head because you promised. The cellarer pays five hundred pennies, six cakes of wax and two bundles of parchment, and you carry away a copy. The saint's boats cross without a pilot that year. The year after, one of them goes on the bank with the leaf open in the steersman's hand. At Witla nobody asks you in.

It takes four days and the boy's hand cramps twice. Pole, lead and tallow, and what each colour of the bottom means. Birds at half ebb. Brown smooth water and wrinkled water. The moon's place for each bar. Last, the rule: at Easter a brother goes out, sounds, and writes what he finds beneath what the last man found. The schoolmaster says it is the first book he has known to admit it will be wrong. Seven hundred pennies, eight cakes of wax, a book for your chest, and the bishop's word that you are Saint Martin's man. At Witla they see the saint's own men sounding the bar, and draw their own conclusion.

Two leaves, the boy writing both and complaining through each. One stays in the book of times. The other you carry down the river in oiled cloth and put into the grandson's hands. He cannot read it. His mother says: then the priest reads it to him at Easter, and he tells the priest where it is wrong. That will do them both good. She keeps your goods on the strand from that day, and counts them. The cellarer's four hundred pennies, wax and parchment are the smaller part of it.
A master for the water

On the dam at Dorestat the marks of the Maas and the Vlie are waited for. The count has a list with a space on it. Thiadbod has a steersman who learns a bar in a tide. Whoever has paid you expects to be told.
The space beside the Maas is still empty, shipman. I have been asked about it by a man who does not like empty spaces, and he was not asking kindly.
A writing for the king's post at Witla: your keel passes untolled for as long as you keep the king's boats off the bank. It lasts as long as you do, and as long as you come when you are called.
A hundred and fifty of my pennies have lived in your purse a long time. I should like to hear them say something.
Twelve hundred pennies more, and the lower end of my dam head: the dry end, with the shed on it. For water. My father would have had me bled.
And the old man? He has an alehouse and a grandson. Most men end with less.
Teach the count's two men the bars, and take the king's writing
Teach Thiadbod's steersman, and take the silver and the dry end of the dam head
Tell them both the old man went blind and the marks went with him, and go down the river to the boy

Two of the count's men row with you for a month, Franks who say 'it' of the river. They learn enough. Your name is written beside the Maas and beside the Vlie; you are given seven hundred pennies and a writing with a seal, and the toll man at Witla lets your keel by with his mouth shut. When the king's boats come to the bar it is you who are sent for, in whatever season it is. On the strand at Witla the old man's grandson is told he may sound the bar when the king's pilot does not need it.

The steersman does not learn it in a tide. He learns it in six weeks, and badly, and that is enough for Thiadbod, whose ships now cross the bar when they please and whose rivals wait. Twelve hundred pennies are counted out on a cask head, and you are walked along the dry end of the dam and shown where your posts may go. At Witla the pilot's house has the old pole and the water has an owner. They do not say which they think is worth more.

You tell them the old man's eyes went and the marks with them: he could not show what he could not see. Thiadbod does not believe a word and cannot prove one. The count has the clerk draw a line through a name. Neither asks for his silver back, since asking would be admitting what it was for. You go down the river. The spring sounding is still to come, and the boy is waiting with the pole.
The pilot of the Maas mouth is going blind, they say at Dorestat. Skippers bound for the sea talk of going round by Walichrum.
There is a new pilot on the bar at Witla: the old man's grandson, with the old man's pole. He sounds everything twice.
At Saint Martin's they have written the bars of the Maas and the Vlie on a leaf, after the chapter on the tides. The saint's steersmen are learning to read.
The count has named a king's pilot for the Maas mouth, a merchant of Dorestat. The pilot's house at Witla was not asked.
Thiadbod's ships cross the bar at Witla without waiting for a pilot now. Everybody else's wait as before.

The door of a turf-walled net shed above a tidal creek on a grey spring morning: a wiry old man in a salt-stiff hooded cloak sits on the sill looking out to a white line of breakers, a notched pole taller than himself against the wall; a woman with a dipper and a small boy stand by; boats sit on the mud below.

A turf mound at the seaward end of a low ridge in hazy noon light, a tall post with a cross-piece on it; the old pilot shades his eyes and looks slightly the wrong way; his daughter beside him points with her chin at a striped sail standing in over brown water.

Inside the net shed on an autumn evening, rain at the open door: the old pilot on an upturned basket holding up three fingers, a merchant sitting on a pile of tarred net, the sounding pole between them, a rush light, his daughter in the doorway with her arms folded.

A small open boat on a river bar at low water on a cold bright spring morning: a merchant in the bow pushing a notched pole into brown water, an old man in the stern with his head on one side holding up a lead with grey sand stuck to its foot, a boy counting on his fingers; gulls standing in a row on a sandbank; a wine ship at anchor outside.

The timber dam at Dorestat on a fine afternoon: a well-fed man with a combed fair beard and a long blue cloak with a silver pin counts pennies onto a cask head, smiling; a young steersman behind him with his thumbs in his belt; a big ship alongside and a small one beyond her.

A creek strand at early morning in summer: a small boat afloat with her sail bent on; the old pilot wading out to her with a pole and a bread bag; his daughter on the sand with folded arms; a boy already half over the bow, looking back at her.

A small boat under a square sail running north in a light summer breeze, a long line of pale dunes on her right hand; far off, a dark squared stone ruin standing in white surf; an old man in the stern with shut eyes and one hand raised, counting lines on his fingers; the steersman looking at the shore.

A narrow flat water between two low green shores under a wide grey sky, a row of thatched houses on a peat bank behind; an eel fisher on the bank mending a wicker trap and pointing west; in a small boat the old pilot sits bowed with his pole across his knees while a merchant looks from one bank to the other.

A plain timber writing room with one small window, afternoon light on a sloping desk: a tonsured schoolmaster with his finger on an open book that shows a drawn moon; a boy scribe with a quill and an ink horn; a merchant in a sea cloak standing, his cap in his hands, sand on the floor from his shoes.

The count's hall at Dorestat by day: a thick-set man with a long moustache and a red cloak pinned on the right shoulder holds out a strip of parchment; a clerk at his elbow with a pen points to an empty place on it; a merchant before them, a toll chest open on the table.

The net shed in low winter light, snow on the turf roof: the old pilot sits inside the door with his face turned towards the listener and his eyes on nothing, hands open on his knees; the pole against the wall; a tall boy outside holding a newer pole; grey sea and the white line of the bar beyond.

A small boat on the bar at Witla on a still spring morning after rain: a long-armed youth in the bow with the old notched pole, a merchant at the oars, and in the stern an old blind man with his face lifted to the wind (or an empty thwart with a folded cloak on it); the ridge, its cross and the mark post behind.

The writing room of Saint Martin's by candle and window light in late autumn: a boy scribe bent over a ruled leaf at the back of a thick book, the schoolmaster reading over his shoulder, a stout cellarer with keys in the doorway, a merchant dictating with a yew stick in his hand; cakes of wax stacked by the wall.

The dam at Dorestat under a windy sky: the count in his red cloak with a sealed writing on one side, the rich skipper in his blue cloak with a heap of pennies on a cask head on the other, a merchant between them looking down river; far off down the water, very small, a boat with a single figure holding a pole.
